lines.text: In the kingdom of Aldmere, one moment decides your whole life.
At sixteen, every noble child places a palm on the Measuring Stone. And the stone shows the depth of their Vessel, the well of power inside them.
One ring of light is a commoner. Three rings, a knight. Five rings, a true lord. Someone who can split a charging warhorse with a single stroke.
The last man to light seven was King Aldric the First. They built a cathedral on the spot.
My older brother Maric lit five. The hall roared. Father wept, which I had only ever seen him do over money.
Then it was my turn. I put my hand on the stone.
Nothing.
Not one ring. Not a flicker. Just cold, black stone, like the bottom of a well.
The silence lasted long enough to hurt. Then someone laughed. Lady Sabine of House Corrow, whose family has wanted our river for three generations.
Oh, how wonderful. An empty Varr.
Well. At least the boy is honest.
Three days later, I was rewarded with Greyhollow.
A northern fief where the frost never fully leaves. A keep with half a roof. Thirty-seven peasants. Six goats. And a debt of four thousand crowns, owed to House Corrow, due at first thaw.
The deed was in my brother's handwriting. At the bottom, he'd added a note. Builds character, little brother.
Welcome to Greyhollow, my lord. Mind the stairs. Or rather, mind where the stairs used to be.
Greyhollow earns maybe two hundred crowns a year. I did the maths. I'll be in debtors' prison by seventeen.
Fine. I can't fight. I can't channel. But I've read every book in my father's library. If my Vessel is empty, my head will have to do the work.
In the ruined kennel, I found a wolfhound. Half starved. One ear torn. Too weak to stand. Everyone had left it to die.
Two failures in one castle. Fine. You're mine now. Your name is Ash.
The dog thumped its tail once. Neither of us noticed the air around us shiver.
That night, far to the south, the Royal Measurer held a lantern over the Measuring Stone, and stopped breathing.
A crack. Straight through its heart.
A stone doesn't crack because it found nothing. It cracks because it couldn't hold what it found.
The last boy who touched this. I want his name.
In the morning, Ash was waiting by the door. His coat had grown in thick and black. His ribs were gone. And at his feet lay a dead frost-wolf, twice the size of a man.
Huh. The soil up here must be good.
That's not how soil works, my lord.
Right. Anyway. Who wants to help me fix a roof?
After I'd gone inside, Bram stood alone in the yard. Out of old habit, he laid his one hand on the village's chipped Measuring Stone. The stone that had shown him a single ring for fifty years.
It lit two.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter two, coming soon.
